videos.title: Notifications Cost You 23 Minutes (Every Single Time)
videos.topic: The hidden cost of notification-driven context switching
videos.summary: Kai starts the day with 240 minutes of real focus. Each notification takes two seconds to read and about 23 minutes to recover from, so the day drains without a single dramatic event.
videos.key_angle: An on-screen focus counter counts down in real time while a narrator explains the researched 23-minute resumption lag — the loss is invisible, not catastrophic.
videos.script_summary: Kai starts the day with 240 minutes of real focus. Each notification takes two seconds to read and about 23 minutes to recover from, so the day drains without a single dramatic event.

videos.title: Discipline vs Obsession: The 9 PM vs 2 AM Problem
videos.topic: Where discipline ends and self-destructive obsession begins
videos.summary: Daniel and Marcus want the same thing and work equally hard. Ten years later one has a life he can sustain and the other has a scoreboard he can never finish.
videos.key_angle: Two parallel ten-year timelines built on the same ambition — the story withholds the verdict until a single phone call to Marcus's mother reframes what he was working for.
videos.script_summary: Daniel and Marcus want the same thing and work equally hard. Ten years later one has a life he can sustain and the other has a scoreboard he can never finish.

videos.title: Procrastination: Why 1 Plank Beats a Whole Bridge
videos.topic: Procrastination as over-planning, and the power of the nearest first step
videos.summary: Mira has drawn the far end of a bridge in perfect detail while the first plank stays blank. Planning feels like movement until she names the nearest edge and steps on it.
videos.key_angle: The far end of the bridge is shown fully finished from the first frame — the obstacle is never the destination, only the blank plank at her feet.
videos.script_summary: Mira has drawn the far end of a bridge in perfect detail while the first plank stays blank. Planning feels like movement until she names the nearest edge and steps on it.

videos.title: Cutting Corners: What a 2-Inch Shortcut Really Costs
videos.topic: Safety margin: why small shortcuts fail when conditions change
videos.summary: Nia shaves two inches off every joint to finish the Kessa bridge five weeks early. In June the river rises four metres and the deck begins to sing.
videos.key_angle: The shortcut is measured in inches and the consequence arrives as weather — the film never moralises, it lets the callipers and the flood do the arguing.
videos.script_summary: Nia shaves two inches off every joint to finish the Kessa bridge five weeks early. In June the river rises four metres and the deck begins to sing.

videos.title: Phone Distraction: The 2-Second Reach That Ends Focus
videos.topic: Designing your environment to beat distraction instead of relying on willpower
videos.summary: An hour is never lost at once — it goes in two-second reaches. Move the phone two steps further away than your impulse and the hour stays yours.
videos.key_angle: The fix is architectural, not motivational: change the room, not your brain. The camera keeps the phone and the hand in the same frame the whole time.
videos.script_summary: An hour is never lost at once — it goes in two-second reaches. Move the phone two steps further away than your impulse and the hour stays yours.

videos.title: 3 AM Anxiety: Why Checking the Clock Makes It Worse
videos.topic: Why 3 AM thoughts feel catastrophic, and how to park them until morning
videos.summary: At 3 AM the rational brain is half asleep and the threat detector is wide awake. Reading the hour invents an emergency — write the worry down and let morning carry it.
videos.key_angle: The villain is the clock itself: reading the time is the event that turns a small tomorrow problem into a verdict on your whole life.
videos.script_summary: At 3 AM the rational brain is half asleep and the threat detector is wide awake. Reading the hour invents an emergency — write the worry down and let morning carry it.

videos.title: Limiting Beliefs: Did You Agree to That Wall?
videos.topic: Limiting beliefs as self-imposed agreements rather than real obstacles
videos.summary: A small ink figure hits a wall and assumes it is permanent. The wall is drawn in dashed ink the whole time — a limit he agreed to, not one that was built.
videos.key_angle: The obstacle is rendered as unfinished dashed brickwork with the landscape visible through it, so the viewer sees it is an agreement before the narration says so.
videos.script_summary: A small ink figure hits a wall and assumes it is permanent. The wall is drawn in dashed ink the whole time — a limit he agreed to, not one that was built.
